source_read: PMC HTML (saved text of PMC4700537, NIH author manuscript), read start to end: abstract, sections 1 to 6, Tables 1 and 2 as rendered text, the Figure 1 legend, abbreviations list, acknowledgments, declaration of interest, publisher's disclaimer and all 153 reference entries. Figure 1 and the chemical structures in Table 2 are images absent from the text. The 'Author information' panel is collapsed in the save, so author affiliations could not be checked; no printed page numbers appear in the HTML.

design.note: narrative-review is right: no methods, search, eligibility criteria or appraisal; a mechanistic survey organised by target system.

key_findings.note: Table 1 as rendered. See 'missed': the table files vasoconstriction and piloerection under heat production, where section 2 and 3.1 treat them as heat retention.
Section 2.3, one paragraph, matches including the direction of the vulnerability (rodents more vulnerable to ambient temperature than humans).
Section 3.2 ¶1-2 and ¶4. The 5-HT2 antagonist named in the paper is ketanserin; the stress findings are Tata et al. 2007 and Doyle & Yamamoto 2010 (rats) against Miller & O'Callaghan 1994 (mice).
Section 4.2 ¶1-2. The threshold above 40 degrees C is cited to a 1978 study of induced hyperthermia in sedated people, which the card's sample field records.
Section 4.2 ¶2 and section 6 ¶1. The card correctly keeps the specific clinical measures out of the finding.
Section 4.3 ¶3, including the authors' own two caveats.

key_findings.correction: Species are conflated in the second half. The beta-adrenoceptor antagonist result (propranolol, Albers & Sonsalla 1995, section 5.1.1 ¶2) is in mice; the sympathectomy, adrenalectomy, glucocorticoid and muscle calcium-release results (Makisumi 1998, section 5.1.1 ¶3) are in rats, and it is that rat series alone that supports the muscle-thermogenesis-under-glucocorticoid-permission reading. The first half (sympathectomy, and catecholamine-synthesis blockade working in rats but not mice and not at the raised ambient temperature) is confirmed at section 5.1 ¶2-3.

key_findings.note: Section 5.1.2 ¶3 to ¶7 as the card says. The exception study is in ICR mice and the review gives its doses as study conditions.

key_findings.correction: Content confirmed, locator off by one at the start: the serotonin-depletion result and the roughly 1 degree C greater response in mice genetically lacking brain serotonin are in section 5.1.3 ¶3, not ¶4 (¶4 is the plasma-serotonin paragraph, which the finding does not cover). The right span is 5.1.3 ¶3 and ¶5 to ¶8.

key_findings.note: Section 5.2, all four strands including the ambient-temperature dependence of the nitric oxide synthase inhibitor results and the older-versus-young rat sensitivity.
Section 5.5, including that the interleukin-1 receptor antagonist reduced deaths without changing temperature and that hypothalamic interleukin-1 beta expression did not track body temperature.

reporting_issues.note: Found independently: 'universal presenting symptom' in the abstract and again in section 1, where the only citation is the agency fact sheet carrying the annual admission count. No series, proportion or temperature distribution appears anywhere in the text.

Confirmed, with one amplification: besides the mouse survivor-versus-died comparison (section 5.1.2 ¶6), section 5.2 reports that older rats show greater sensitivity to the hyperthermic and lethal effects, and section 5.1.2 ¶7 a higher lethal dose in transporter knockout mice. All are animal data, so the card's point stands.

Section 3.2 ¶1. Worth adding that the sentence is circular as printed (65% of heat-related deaths resulting from exposure to excessive heat), and that the methamphetamine inference is explicitly an expectation by analogy with MDMA.

Both checked against the reference list: it contains Bowyer et al. 1992, 1994 and 2013 and Bowyer & Holson 1995, and no 1984 or 'Bowyer et al. 1995' entry. The emergency-room sentence (section 4.2 ¶1) cites only that untraceable 1984 item and a mouse study, so it has no human source at all.

Confirmed across the whole paper: the roughly 1 degree C figure is the only magnitude for any experiment; elsewhere only direction words are used. Animal doses and ambient temperatures appear only sporadically, as the card says.
Section 5.1.3 ¶3 reads as the card describes; the phrase about treating mice with the enzyme itself is almost certainly a dropped word, and the sentence cannot be paraphrased safely.

Both spellings confirmed in text and Table 2; the reference list also prints one cited author's surname two ways (text 'Beauvais', list 'Beavais'), and the list has further typographical errors in titles.

Confirmed: read from the author manuscript with the publisher's disclaimer, no printed pagination in the HTML, header date 14 May 2014. Not checkable here: that the print issue is October 2014; the saved text gives only the May 2014 date. Either way the citation year is 2014.

risk_of_bias.note: Wrong instrument for the design, as on sc_hemphill_2024. The card is labelled narrative-review but appraised with AMSTAR 2; METHODS §5.3 requires the editors' narrative-review checklist with instrument 'none-applicable', and scripts/rob_vocab.py flags the mismatch. Proposed checklist judgments: systematic search and explicit selection = high (none reported); appraisal of the cited studies = high (no appraisal of any kind, and no SYRCLE-type consideration of randomization, blinding or sample size in the animal literature that makes up nearly the whole evidence base); reliance on the authors' own work = some concerns (the sigma-receptor compounds offered in Table 2 as potential therapeutic options come from the corresponding author's programme, and two co-authors wrote several of the cited temperature-and-neurotoxicity studies); separation of evidence from speculation = some concerns (the body is explicit about what is unknown, but the abstract states two human generalizations the body does not support, and section 3.2 extrapolates to people prescribed stimulants without evidence); balance = low (a dedicated section on manipulations that did nothing, species differences and contradictory findings reported throughout). Overall = high, the worst domain. The card's AMSTAR reasoning carries over unchanged in substance, including that nothing here can anchor a quantitative claim.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' is defensible and I agree, though a reader could argue for 'minor' because the gap is confined to two sentences. Both are in the abstract, both are about people, and both are contradicted in spirit by the body, which says the basis of the effect is largely unknown and unexplored; the abstract is what gets quoted.

missed: Table 1 files vasoconstriction and piloerection under 'activation of heat production mechanisms' for methamphetamine, whereas section 2 lists vasoconstriction and insulation as heat retention strategies and section 3.1 describes vasoconstriction as preventing heat dissipation. An internal inconsistency in the paper's own framing; it should be a reporting issue, since the table is the part most likely to be reused.

Several citations in section 3.1 do not support the statements they are attached to: the sentence that methamphetamine causes vasoconstriction cites an MDMA thermoregulation study in rats, an emergency-department study of chest pain, a myocardial infarction case report and an electrocardiographic study, none of which measured vasoconstriction; the saliva-spreading statement cites a general thermoregulation review. This belongs with the citation problems already recorded as reporting issue 3.

Section 4.1 is not represented in the key findings. Its substantive point for this card is the authors' statement that it is unclear whether maximum temperature elevation tracks peak plasma concentration or cumulative exposure, and that a metabolite can itself raise body temperature. That is the paper's own acknowledgement that no dose-temperature relation is established, which supports cannot_establish and should be anchored there (without the route and bioavailability figures, which are not needed for any claim).

Table 2 labels the serotonin-releasing drug discussed in section 5.1.3 ¶7 as a transporter inhibitor, while the text calls it an indirect agonist acting through several mechanisms and notes it also releases noradrenaline. A text-table inconsistency of the same kind as the spelling issues already listed.

Section 3.2 ¶3 extends the heat argument to children and adults treated for ADHD with amphetamine salts and to sport in hot weather. No evidence is offered, and this is a clinical extrapolation about a different substance and population; it should be flagged so that no monograph picks it up from this review.
other_notes: Reference count 153 confirmed by counting the list.

funding.affiliations_note (West Virginia University, University of Chicago, Vanderbilt, NIOSH) could not be checked: the affiliation panel is collapsed in the saved text. The acknowledgment of the two NIH grants and the no-conflicts declaration are confirmed.

sample.recruitment and analysis.effect_sizes are accurate as written, including the two human figures and the species list (rats, several mouse lines, rhesus macaques, isolated hepatocytes and synaptosomes).

One cited source in the reference list is marked as retracted by PMC (a 2011 journal article on heat shock protein expression during acute intoxication, cited in sections 3.2 and 6). The card does not note it. METHODS §4.3 concerns the encyclopedia's own references rather than a review's citations, but a reader relying on this review's mechanism section should know.
